P.title: P.blurb
Artificial Intelligence: How machines learn and what's really inside a chatbot, explained without maths homework.

P.title: ai-learn.summary
Artificial Intelligence: No magic: examples, a lot of simple maths and millions of small corrections.

P.title: ai-learn.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: What does a machine-learning model learn from?

P.title: ai-learn.q0.o2
Artificial Intelligence: The internet's search results at runtime

P.title: ai-learn.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: It finds patterns in example data. Nobody writes the rules by hand.

P.title: ai-learn.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: Sunny (+3) and raining (−4), not a weekend, bias −2. Does the beach neuron fire?

P.title: ai-learn.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: 3 − 4 − 2 = −3, which is below zero, so no.

P.title: ai-learn.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: A model scores 100% on its training data but badly on new data. That's…

P.title: ai-learn.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: It memorised the examples instead of the general pattern.

P.title: ai-learn.q3.q
Artificial Intelligence: What is the test set for?

P.title: ai-learn.q3.o2
Artificial Intelligence: A final, honest check on unseen data

P.title: ai-learn.q3.x
Artificial Intelligence: It is kept aside and only used once, so the score reflects new data.

P.title: ai-learn.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: Try writing rules that recognise a cat: pointy ears, whiskers… but foxes have those too, and some cats hide their ears. You'd never finish.\n\nMachine learning flips it around. You show the computer thousands of labelled photos and let it work out the patterns itself. The result is called a model.

P.title: ai-learn.c1.title
Artificial Intelligence: A neuron is a weighted vote

P.title: ai-learn.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: The building block of a neural network is tiny. It takes a few inputs, multiplies each by a weight (how much it matters), adds them up and says yes if the total is high enough.\n\nShould you go to the beach? Sunny counts +3, weekend +2, rain −4. Stack millions of these little votes in layers and you get a network that can recognise faces or write text.

P.title: ai-learn.c1.sketch.8
Artificial Intelligence: add up the votes: positive means yes

P.title: ai-learn.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Switch the inputs on and off. The neuron adds up input × weight, plus a small bias of −2 (it needs a reason to go), and fires when the total is above zero.

P.title: ai-learn.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: A new network starts with random weights and makes terrible guesses. Training repeats a simple loop: make a guess, measure how wrong it was, then nudge every weight a tiny bit in the direction that reduces the error.\n\nPicture a ball rolling downhill into the valley of lowest error. Large models repeat this billions of times.

P.title: ai-learn.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: A model can fit its training examples perfectly and still be useless, like a student who memorised last year's exam answers. This is called overfitting.\n\nThe fix is to test on examples the model has never seen. If it does well there too, it has learned the real pattern rather than the noise.

P.title: ai-learn.c4.sketch.2
Artificial Intelligence: new data follows the blue line

P.title: ai-learn.c5.title
Artificial Intelligence: Features: what the model looks at

P.title: ai-learn.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: A model never sees "a house". It sees numbers that describe it, called features: floor area, number of bedrooms, distance to the coast, year built.\n\nChoosing good features used to be most of the work. Deep learning learns many of them by itself, but the idea stays the same: the model can only use what you give it.

P.title: ai-learn.c5.viz.steps.0
Artificial Intelligence: 120 m², 3 bedrooms, 2 km to the coast

P.title: ai-learn.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: You split your data before training. The model learns from the training set, you tune settings on the validation set, and the test set stays locked away until the very end.\n\nIf you peek at the test set while building the model, your final score will be too optimistic.

P.title: ai-learn.c7.title
Artificial Intelligence: The simplest model: a straight line

P.title: ai-learn.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: With one feature, a model can be a line. It multiplies the input by a weight and adds a bias. Training finds the weight and bias that make the line fit the data best.\n\nNeural networks are millions of these little sums stacked together, with a twist added between them.

P.title: ai-learn.c8.title
Artificial Intelligence: More data often beats a cleverer algorithm

P.title: ai-learn.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: In many real problems, a simple model trained on a lot of good data outperforms a sophisticated model trained on a little. Google researchers called this "the unreasonable effectiveness of data" in 2009.\n\nQuality matters as much as quantity: a million mislabelled examples teach the wrong lesson very confidently.

P.title: ai-learn.c9.title
Artificial Intelligence: A spam filter, step by step

P.title: ai-learn.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: Every incoming email is turned into features: words used, sender reputation, number of links. The model outputs a score between 0 and 1. Above a threshold, say 0.9, it goes to spam.\n\nChoosing that threshold is a business decision: lower it and you catch more spam but lose more real emails.

P.title: ai-chat.summary
Artificial Intelligence: What's really going on inside ChatGPT, Claude and friends.

P.title: ai-chat.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: What does a language model actually do at each step?

P.title: ai-chat.q0.o0
Artificial Intelligence: Looks the answer up in a database

P.title: ai-chat.q0.o1
Artificial Intelligence: Predicts the most likely next token

P.title: ai-chat.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: It estimates probabilities for the next token, picks one, and repeats.

P.title: ai-chat.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: Roughly how many English words fit in 1,000 tokens?

P.title: ai-chat.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: A token averages about ¾ of a word in English.

P.title: ai-chat.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: You want consistent, predictable answers. Which temperature?

P.title: ai-chat.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: Low temperature concentrates the odds on the most likely tokens.

P.title: ai-chat.q3.q
Artificial Intelligence: Why might a chatbot not know about yesterday's news?

P.title: ai-chat.q3.o1
Artificial Intelligence: Its knowledge stops at a training cutoff unless it has a search tool

P.title: ai-chat.q3.x
Artificial Intelligence: Without tools, a model only knows what was in its training data.

P.title: ai-chat.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: Language models don't read letters or whole words. Text is chopped into tokens: common words stay whole, rarer ones are split into pieces. Each token is just a number to the model.\n\nIn English a token averages about ¾ of a word, which is why AI services price and limit usage in tokens.

P.title: ai-chat.c0.sketch.7
Artificial Intelligence: token numbers are made up for this example

P.title: ai-chat.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: At heart, a language model does one thing: given the text so far, it estimates how likely each possible next token is. It picks one, adds it to the text and repeats.\n\nTrained on a huge amount of writing, that simple trick ends up capturing grammar, facts, styles and a surprising amount of reasoning.

P.title: ai-chat.c1.sketch.9
Artificial Intelligence: it picks from these odds, one word at a time

P.title: ai-chat.c2.title
Artificial Intelligence: Try it: turn up the temperature

P.title: ai-chat.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Temperature controls how adventurous the model is. Low temperature almost always picks the top word; high temperature spreads the odds so rarer words get a chance. Press Generate a few times at each setting.

P.title: ai-chat.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: Inside the model, every token becomes a list of numbers called an embedding, like coordinates on a map of meaning. Similar ideas sit close together: cat near dog, Lisbon near Porto.\n\nDirections carry meaning too. The step from 'man' to 'woman' is roughly the same as from 'king' to 'queen'.

P.title: ai-chat.c4.title
Artificial Intelligence: Fluent isn't the same as true

P.title: ai-chat.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: Because a model predicts plausible text, it can produce confident sentences that are simply wrong. People call this hallucination. It's most likely with exact numbers, dates, quotes and niche facts.\n\nUse AI for drafting, explaining and brainstorming, and check anything important against a reliable source. (The Eiffel Tower was finished in 1889.)

P.title: ai-chat.c4.sketch.3
Artificial Intelligence: sounds sure, still wrong: check key facts

P.title: ai-chat.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: A model can only "see" a limited amount of text at once, measured in tokens. This is its context window: your question, the conversation so far and any documents you pasted.\n\nWhen a conversation grows past the limit, the oldest parts are dropped or summarised. Windows have grown enormously since 2022.

P.title: ai-chat.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: First the model reads a huge amount of text and learns to predict the next token. That makes it knowledgeable but not yet helpful.\n\nThen it is fine-tuned on examples of good answers, and trained further with human (and AI) feedback on which responses are better. That is what turns a text predictor into an assistant.

P.title: ai-chat.c6.viz.steps.0
Artificial Intelligence: Read vast text, predict next token

P.title: ai-chat.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: The model only knows what you tell it. Say who you are, what you need, what good looks like and in what format. Paste the relevant data instead of describing it. If the first answer is off, say what to change.

P.title: ai-chat.c7.viz.items.0
Artificial Intelligence: Give context: who it's for and why

P.title: ai-chat.c7.viz.items.3
Artificial Intelligence: Ask for a format: table, bullets, length

P.title: ai-chat.c8.title
Artificial Intelligence: Models don't look things up by themselves

P.title: ai-chat.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: A plain language model answers from what it learned during training, which stops at a cutoff date. It doesn't know today's news or your files.\n\nModern assistants are given tools: web search, document access, code execution. With tools, they can fetch fresh facts instead of guessing.

P.title: ai-chat.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: Model sizes are counted in parameters, the learned weights. A 70B model has 70 billion of them. Stored in 16-bit format, each weight takes 2 bytes, so the model alone needs about 140 GB of memory.\n\nThat's why big models run in data centres, and why smaller or compressed (quantised) models run on laptops.

P.title: ai-types.summary
Artificial Intelligence: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, and when each fits.

P.title: ai-types.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: Predicting tomorrow's electricity demand in kWh is…

P.title: ai-types.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: A number is being predicted, so it's regression.

P.title: ai-types.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: An AI that learns chess by playing millions of games against itself uses…

P.title: ai-types.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: It learns from wins and losses, which are rewards.

P.title: ai-types.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: Hiding a word in a sentence and asking the model to guess it is…

P.title: ai-types.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: The data provides its own labels.

P.title: ai-types.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: You give the model examples with the right answers attached: photos labelled "cat" or "dog", houses with their sale price. It learns to map inputs to answers.\n\nIt's the most common kind of machine learning in business: forecasting, fraud detection, document classification.

P.title: ai-types.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Supervised problems come in two flavours. Classification picks a category: spam or not, which product type, which disease. Regression predicts a number: tomorrow's price, delivery time, energy demand.

P.title: ai-types.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Here there are no labels. The model looks for structure on its own: groups of similar customers, unusual transactions, topics in a pile of documents.\n\nIt's useful when you don't yet know what you're looking for, or labelling would be too expensive.

P.title: ai-types.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: Give a clustering algorithm the purchase history of 100,000 customers and ask for five groups. It might find bargain hunters, weekend shoppers, big occasional buyers and so on.\n\nThe algorithm finds the groups; a human still has to look at them and decide what they mean.

P.title: ai-types.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: An agent learns by trial and error. It takes an action, the environment responds, and it receives a reward or penalty. Over millions of attempts it learns which actions lead to the most reward.\n\nThis is how computers learned to play Go, chess and video games better than humans.

P.title: ai-types.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: A clever trick: create the labels from the data itself. Hide a word in a sentence and ask the model to guess it. Hide part of an image and ask it to fill in the gap.\n\nNo humans needed to label anything, so you can train on billions of examples. Large language models are trained this way.

P.title: ai-types.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: Supervised learning needs labelled data, and labelling is slow human work. Medical images need doctors; legal documents need lawyers.\n\nThat cost is why self-supervised pre-training became so important: learn general knowledge from unlabelled data first, then fine-tune with a small labelled set.

P.title: ai-types.c7.title
Artificial Intelligence: Semi-supervised: a little help goes far

P.title: ai-types.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: Often you have a few labelled examples and a mountain of unlabelled ones. Semi-supervised methods use the labelled ones to get started, then let the model label the rest, keeping only its confident guesses.

P.title: ai-types.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: Have past examples with known outcomes? Supervised. Want to discover structure? Unsupervised. Is it a sequence of decisions with a goal, like a game or a robot? Reinforcement.

P.title: ai-types.c8.viz.root
Artificial Intelligence: Do you have the right answers?

P.title: ai-types.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: Despite the headlines about game-playing and chatbots, most deployed machine learning in companies is still supervised: predicting churn, demand, defaults or delays from historical records.

P.title: ai-data.summary
Artificial Intelligence: Where training data comes from and how it goes wrong.

P.title: ai-data.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: A model looks perfect in testing but fails in production. A likely cause is…

P.title: ai-data.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: Leakage gives the model information during training that it won't have in real use.

P.title: ai-data.q1.o1
Artificial Intelligence: The real world changing so old training data no longer matches

P.title: ai-data.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: Patterns shift over time, so models need monitoring and retraining.

P.title: ai-data.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: Text, images and audio don't fit neatly into rows and columns.

P.title: ai-data.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: A model is a summary of its training data. If the data is wrong, incomplete or skewed, the model will be too, and it will be wrong with great confidence.\n\nIn real projects, preparing data usually takes more time than building the model.

P.title: ai-data.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Surveys of data scientists consistently find that collecting, cleaning and organising data takes the largest share of their time. Training the model is often the quick part.

P.title: ai-data.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Structured data fits in tables: transactions, sensor readings, ERP records. Unstructured data is everything else: emails, contracts, photos, audio.\n\nClassic machine learning loves tables. Deep learning made unstructured data usable at scale.

P.title: ai-data.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: Real data has gaps: a sensor went offline, a field was left empty. You can drop those rows, fill them with an average, or let the model treat "missing" as information in itself.\n\nSometimes the fact that a value is missing says something, like a customer who never gave a phone number.

P.title: ai-data.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: Leakage happens when the training data contains information the model won't have when it's used for real. A churn model trained with a "cancellation date" column will look brilliant in testing and fail in production.\n\nAlways ask: would I know this value at the moment I make the prediction?

P.title: ai-data.c4.viz.items.0.r
Artificial Intelligence: use only data known before the decision

P.title: ai-data.c4.viz.items.1.r
Artificial Intelligence: split by date: past trains, future tests

P.title: ai-data.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: If your data doesn't represent the people or situations the model will meet, it will fail on the ones it never saw. A face detector trained mostly on one group performs worse on others.

P.title: ai-data.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: The world changes and models trained on last year's data slowly go stale. Customer behaviour shifts, prices change, a new product appears.\n\nThat's why deployed models need monitoring and periodic retraining.

P.title: ai-data.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: When real data is scarce or private, you can generate artificial examples: simulated sensor faults, fake but realistic invoices, rendered images.\n\nIt helps, but synthetic data only contains the patterns you put into it. Always test on real data.

P.title: ai-data.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: Personal data used for training falls under laws such as the EU's GDPR. You need a legal basis, should collect only what's needed, and must protect it.\n\nAnonymising data is harder than it looks: combining a few fields like postcode, birth date and gender can identify many people.

P.title: ai-data.c8.viz.items.4
Artificial Intelligence: Keep a record of where it came from

P.title: ai-data.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: Labels are created by people, and people disagree or make mistakes. Good projects write clear labelling guidelines, have several people label the same examples, and measure how often they agree.

P.title: ai-algos.summary
Artificial Intelligence: The workhorses that still run much of business AI.

P.title: ai-algos.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: Which method builds trees one after another, each fixing the previous ones' errors?

P.title: ai-algos.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: Boosting is sequential; random forests are independent trees that vote.

P.title: ai-algos.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: Logistic regression is mainly used for…

P.title: ai-algos.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: It outputs a probability for a yes/no outcome.

P.title: ai-algos.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: For a table of sales data, a strong first choice is often…

P.title: ai-algos.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: Boosted trees are fast and accurate on tabular data.

P.title: ai-algos.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: The oldest trick: draw the best straight line through the data. It predicts a number from a weighted sum of the inputs.\n\nIt's fast, easy to explain ("each extra m² adds €2,500") and often a strong baseline before trying anything fancier.

P.title: ai-algos.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Despite the name, it's for classification. It squeezes a weighted sum into a probability between 0 and 1 using an S-shaped curve. Above 0.5 means "yes".\n\nBanks have used it for decades for credit scoring because every weight can be explained.

P.title: ai-algos.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: A tree asks a series of yes/no questions: Is income above €30k? Has the customer missed a payment? Each path ends in a prediction.\n\nTrees are easy to read and explain, but a single tree tends to overfit.

P.title: ai-algos.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: Train hundreds of slightly different decision trees on random slices of the data, then let them vote. The crowd is far more accurate and stable than any single tree.

P.title: ai-algos.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: Instead of trees voting independently, boosting builds them in sequence. Each new tree focuses on the mistakes of the ones before it.\n\nLibraries like XGBoost and LightGBM win many competitions on tabular data and are widely used in industry.

P.title: ai-algos.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: To classify something new, find the k most similar examples you already know and take a vote. A new house is priced like its five most similar neighbours.\n\nSimple and intuitive, but slow when the dataset is huge.

P.title: ai-algos.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: An unsupervised classic. Pick k centre points, assign every item to its nearest centre, move each centre to the middle of its group, and repeat until nothing changes.

P.title: ai-algos.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: For tables of numbers, such as sales, prices or sensor logs, gradient-boosted trees often match or beat neural networks, train faster and are easier to explain.\n\nNeural networks shine with images, audio and text.

P.title: ai-algos.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: Before building anything complex, measure a dumb baseline: "predict the average" or "same as last week". If your clever model barely beats it, it's not worth deploying.

P.title: ai-algos.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: Think about the data type, how much data you have, whether you must explain decisions, and how fast predictions need to be. In practice, teams try a few and pick by measured results.

P.title: ai-algos.c9.viz.items.0
Artificial Intelligence: What kind of data: table, text, image?

P.title: ai-nets.summary
Artificial Intelligence: Layers, activations and how the network learns from its mistakes.

P.title: ai-nets.q0.o1
Artificial Intelligence: Works out how each weight contributed to the error

P.title: ai-nets.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: It sends the error backwards so every weight can be adjusted.

P.title: ai-nets.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: A learning rate that is too high causes…

P.title: ai-nets.q1.o0
Artificial Intelligence: Training that jumps around and may never settle

P.title: ai-nets.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: One full pass through the training data is called…

P.title: ai-nets.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: An epoch is one complete pass; batches are the small chunks within it.

P.title: ai-nets.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: A neural network is organised in layers. The input layer receives the data, hidden layers transform it step by step, and the output layer gives the answer.\n\n"Deep" learning simply means many hidden layers.

P.title: ai-nets.c0.viz.steps.1
Artificial Intelligence: Hidden layers find edges, shapes, parts

P.title: ai-nets.c1.title
Artificial Intelligence: Each layer learns more abstract features

P.title: ai-nets.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: In an image network, early layers detect edges and colours. Middle layers combine them into textures and shapes. Later layers recognise eyes, wheels or faces.\n\nNobody programs these features; they emerge from training.

P.title: ai-nets.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Between layers, each neuron passes its sum through an activation function. The most common, ReLU, simply turns negative values into zero.\n\nWithout this non-linear step, stacking layers would collapse into one big straight-line model.

P.title: ai-nets.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: To learn, the network needs a score for how wrong it is. That's the loss. For a price prediction, it might be the average squared error; for classification, how little probability it gave the right answer.\n\nTraining is the search for weights that make the loss as small as possible.

P.title: ai-nets.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: After a wrong guess, the error is sent backwards through the network. Using calculus, each weight learns how much it contributed to the mistake and in which direction to move.\n\nThis algorithm, popularised in 1986, is how virtually every neural network is trained today.

P.title: ai-nets.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: How big should each nudge be? That's the learning rate. Too small and training takes forever. Too large and the model overshoots the valley and never settles.

P.title: ai-nets.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: Training data is fed in small batches, say 32 examples at a time, and the weights are updated after each batch. One full pass through all the data is an epoch. Networks often train for many epochs.

P.title: ai-nets.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: To stop a network memorising, you can randomly switch off some neurons during training (dropout) or penalise very large weights. The network is forced to learn patterns that are robust, not fragile shortcuts.

P.title: ai-nets.c7.viz.items.2
Artificial Intelligence: Early stopping: stop when validation stops improving

P.title: ai-nets.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: A convolutional layer slides a small filter, say 3×3 pixels, across the image, looking for the same pattern everywhere: an edge, a curve, a texture. It's why image networks recognise a cat in any corner of the photo.

P.title: ai-nets.c8.viz.steps.2
Artificial Intelligence: Map of where the pattern appears

P.title: ai-nets.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: Training means multiplying huge grids of numbers, over and over. Graphics cards were built to do thousands of simple calculations in parallel for video games, which turned out to be exactly what neural networks need.

P.title: ai-nets.c9.viz.r.items.1
Artificial Intelligence: same sum on lots of data

P.title: ai-metrics.summary
Artificial Intelligence: Accuracy, precision, recall and why one number is never enough.

P.title: ai-metrics.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: 50 real fraud cases exist; the model catches 40. Recall is…

P.title: ai-metrics.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: Which metric answers "of the alerts raised, how many were real?"

P.title: ai-metrics.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: Precision measures how trustworthy the alerts are.

P.title: ai-metrics.q2.o1
Artificial Intelligence: When the positive class is rare, always guessing 'no' scores high

P.title: ai-metrics.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: With 1% fraud, a do-nothing model is 99% accurate.

P.title: ai-metrics.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: If 1% of transactions are fraud, a model that always says "not fraud" is 99% accurate and completely useless.\n\nWhen one outcome is rare, accuracy hides the failures you care about most.

P.title: ai-metrics.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Every prediction lands in one of four boxes: true positives (caught), false positives (false alarms), false negatives (missed) and true negatives (correctly ignored).\n\nMost useful metrics are built from these four counts.

P.title: ai-metrics.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Of everything the model flagged, how much was right? High precision means few false alarms.

P.title: ai-metrics.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: Of all the real cases, how many did the model catch? High recall means few misses.

P.title: ai-metrics.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: Lower the alarm threshold and you catch more (recall up) but raise more false alarms (precision down). Raise it and the opposite happens. Where to set it is a business choice.

P.title: ai-metrics.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: F1 combines precision and recall into one number, their harmonic mean. It is high only when both are high.

P.title: ai-metrics.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: For regression, you measure how far predictions land from reality. MAE is the average absolute error ("off by €8,000 on average"). RMSE punishes big misses more. MAPE gives the error as a percentage.

P.title: ai-metrics.c6.viz.items.2.b
Artificial Intelligence: error as a % of the true value

P.title: ai-metrics.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: A forecast with 10% error sounds good until you learn that "same as last week" gets 11%. Always report your model next to a simple baseline and the current human process.

P.title: ai-metrics.c8.title
Artificial Intelligence: Test like it will be used

P.title: ai-metrics.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: Evaluate on data that looks like the future: later dates, new customers, other regions. Then keep monitoring after launch, because the real test starts on day one in production.

P.title: ai-metrics.c9.title
Artificial Intelligence: Measure what matters to the business

P.title: ai-metrics.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: A model that's 2% more accurate but takes 10 seconds per prediction, or can't be explained to a regulator, may be worse. Translate errors into money, time or risk.

P.title: ai-vision.summary
Artificial Intelligence: How machines see: pixels, convolutions and object detection.

P.title: ai-vision.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: Drawing labelled boxes around every person and car in an image is…

P.title: ai-vision.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: Detection locates each object with a box.

P.title: ai-vision.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: Fine-tuning a model pre-trained on millions of images with your own few hundred photos is called…

P.title: ai-vision.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: You transfer what it already learned to your task.

P.title: ai-vision.q2.o1
Artificial Intelligence: It won ImageNet by a large margin and sparked the deep-learning boom

P.title: ai-vision.q2.o2
Artificial Intelligence: It recognised faces for the first time

P.title: ai-vision.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: Its error was far lower than previous methods.

P.title: ai-vision.c0.title
Artificial Intelligence: An image is a grid of numbers

P.title: ai-vision.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: To a computer, a photo is a grid of pixels, each stored as three numbers for red, green and blue, from 0 to 255. A 12-megapixel phone photo is about 36 million numbers.

P.title: ai-vision.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: The simplest vision task: what's in this picture? The network outputs a probability for each category it knows.

P.title: ai-vision.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Detection goes further: it finds every object and draws a box around each one, with a label and a confidence score. It's what security camera systems such as Frigate use to tell a person from a passing car or a cat.

P.title: ai-vision.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: Segmentation labels every single pixel: road, car, pedestrian, sky. Self-driving cars and medical imaging rely on it to know exact shapes, not just boxes.

P.title: ai-vision.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: ImageNet is a dataset of over 14 million labelled images. In 2012, a deep network called AlexNet won its yearly competition by a huge margin, cutting the error rate from about 26% to 15%. That result kicked off the deep-learning boom.

P.title: ai-vision.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: You rarely train a vision model from scratch. You take one already trained on millions of images and fine-tune it on a few hundred of your own, such as photos of defective parts.

P.title: ai-vision.c5.viz.steps.0
Artificial Intelligence: Model trained on millions of images

P.title: ai-vision.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: OCR turns pictures of text into text: scanned invoices, number plates, signs. Modern OCR also understands layout, so it knows which number is the total and which is the date.

P.title: ai-vision.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: Many cameras now run detection locally on small accelerators instead of sending video to the cloud. That's faster, cheaper and keeps footage private.

P.title: ai-vision.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: Vision models can be fooled by unusual lighting, angles, rain on the lens or objects they never saw in training. A model trained in summer may struggle with snow.\n\nTest in the real conditions where the camera will live.

P.title: ai-vision.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: Face recognition identifies specific people and is legally sensitive. Under the EU AI Act, real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces by police is prohibited except in narrow, authorised cases.

P.title: ai-speech.summary
Artificial Intelligence: How machines hear, transcribe and talk back.

P.title: ai-speech.q0.o1
Artificial Intelligence: A picture of which frequencies are loud over time

P.title: ai-speech.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: It turns audio into an image-like grid.

P.title: ai-speech.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: Why do smart speakers detect the wake word on the device?

P.title: ai-speech.q1.o0
Artificial Intelligence: It's illegal to use the cloud

P.title: ai-speech.q1.o1
Artificial Intelligence: It's fast, cheap and keeps everyday audio private

P.title: ai-speech.q1.o2
Artificial Intelligence: The cloud can't understand wake words

P.title: ai-speech.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: Only after the wake word is audio sent onward.

P.title: ai-speech.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: What's the safest response to an urgent payment request in a manager's voice?

P.title: ai-speech.q2.o1
Artificial Intelligence: Verify through a known, separate channel

P.title: ai-speech.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: Voices can be cloned; verification must not depend on the call itself.

P.title: ai-speech.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: Audio is a wave of air pressure, sampled thousands of times per second. AI models usually convert it into a spectrogram: a picture of which frequencies are loud at each moment. Then image-style techniques can be applied.

P.title: ai-speech.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Phone calls are typically sampled 8,000 times per second, which is enough for speech. CDs use 44,100, enough to capture everything humans can hear (up to about 20 kHz).

P.title: ai-speech.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) turns speech into words. Modern systems are trained on hundreds of thousands of hours of audio and handle accents, noise and multiple languages.\n\nOpenAI's open Whisper model, released in 2022, was trained on 680,000 hours.

P.title: ai-speech.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: TTS works the other way round. Neural voices now sound natural, with breathing and emphasis. Some can clone a voice from a short sample, which raises fraud concerns.

P.title: ai-speech.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: A voice assistant chains several models: a small one listens for the wake word, ASR transcribes the request, a language model works out the intent, and TTS speaks the answer.

P.title: ai-speech.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: Your phone or smart speaker isn't sending everything to the cloud. A tiny model on the device listens only for "Hey…". Only after it triggers does audio leave the device.

P.title: ai-speech.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: In a meeting recording, diarisation answers "who spoke when?". Combined with transcription, it produces minutes with names attached.

P.title: ai-speech.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: Audio AI also recognises other sounds: a glass breaking, a baby crying, a machine bearing starting to fail. Predictive maintenance often listens for changes in vibration and noise.

P.title: ai-speech.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: With a few seconds of someone's voice, modern tools can make convincing fake audio. Scammers have used cloned voices of executives to request urgent payments.\n\nAgree on verification steps for any unusual payment request, whatever the voice sounds like.

P.title: ai-speech.c8.viz.items.0.r
Artificial Intelligence: call back on a known number

P.title: ai-speech.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: Combine speech recognition, machine translation and speech synthesis and you get near real-time spoken translation. Some systems now translate speech directly without writing text in between.

P.title: ai-recs.summary
Artificial Intelligence: How Netflix, Amazon and Spotify decide what to show you.

P.title: ai-recs.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: Users who liked this also liked… describes…

P.title: ai-recs.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: It relies on similar users' behaviour.

P.title: ai-recs.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: A new product with no ratings yet is an example of…

P.title: ai-recs.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: There's no history to learn from yet.

P.title: ai-recs.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: Comparing two recommenders on live users, half each, is…

P.title: ai-recs.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: A shop may have a million products; you'll look at a few dozen. Recommenders predict which few you're most likely to want, from your history and from people like you.

P.title: ai-recs.c0.viz.steps.1
Artificial Intelligence: Narrow to a few hundred candidates

P.title: ai-recs.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: People who bought this also bought… The system finds users with similar tastes to yours and recommends what they liked. It needs no understanding of the products themselves.

P.title: ai-recs.c1.viz.r.items.0
Artificial Intelligence: liked A, B, C and D

P.title: ai-recs.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: This approach looks at the items: genre, author, ingredients, price range. If you read three thriller novels, it suggests more thrillers.

P.title: ai-recs.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: A brand-new user or product has no history, so collaborative filtering has nothing to work with. Systems fall back on popularity, ask a few questions, or use item content until data arrives.

P.title: ai-recs.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: Explicit feedback is a star rating. Implicit feedback is behaviour: clicks, time spent, songs skipped, items returned. Implicit data is far more plentiful, so most systems rely on it.

P.title: ai-recs.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: Netflix has reported that around 80% of what members watch is discovered through its recommendations rather than search. Recommenders shape what millions of people see each day.

P.title: ai-recs.c5.viz.items.0.l
Artificial Intelligence: of Netflix viewing comes from recommendations (company figure)

P.title: ai-recs.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: If a system only shows you more of what you already clicked, your feed narrows. Good recommenders deliberately mix in some variety and new items, a balance called exploration versus exploitation.

P.title: ai-recs.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: Modern recommenders turn every user and item into a list of numbers, an embedding. Items close together on this map are similar; a user's position shows their taste.

P.title: ai-recs.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: Offline, teams check if the model would have predicted what users actually clicked. Online, they run A/B tests: half the users see the new system, and they compare clicks, purchases or retention.

P.title: ai-recs.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: The same techniques suggest jobs on LinkedIn, friends on social networks, articles in news apps, and even which spare part a technician will need.

P.title: ai-rl.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: What makes chess hard for reinforcement learning?

P.title: ai-rl.q0.o1
Artificial Intelligence: The reward only arrives at the end of the game

P.title: ai-rl.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: Credit must be assigned to earlier moves.

P.title: ai-rl.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: An agent exploiting a loophole to get points without doing the task is…

P.title: ai-rl.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: Why do robots often learn in simulation first?

P.title: ai-rl.q2.o1
Artificial Intelligence: It's faster, cheaper and safe to fail

P.title: ai-rl.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: Millions of trials would wear out a real robot.

P.title: ai-rl.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: Reinforcement learning has three ingredients: an agent that acts, an environment that responds, and a reward signal that says how well it's doing. The agent's goal is to maximise total reward over time.

P.title: ai-rl.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Should the agent repeat what worked before, or try something new that might work better? Too little exploration and it gets stuck; too much and it never cashes in.

P.title: ai-rl.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: In chess, the reward only comes at the end: win or lose. The agent must work out which of its earlier moves deserve the credit. This "credit assignment" is what makes RL hard.

P.title: ai-rl.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: Go has more possible positions than there are atoms in the observable universe. In 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, one of the world's best players, 4–1. Its successor, AlphaZero, learned purely by playing against itself.

P.title: ai-rl.c3.viz.events.0.l
Artificial Intelligence: Deep Blue beats Kasparov at chess

P.title: ai-rl.c3.viz.events.1.l
Artificial Intelligence: AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol at Go

P.title: ai-rl.c3.viz.events.3.l
Artificial Intelligence: AlphaStar reaches top level in StarCraft II

P.title: ai-rl.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: An agent can be its own opponent. Each new version plays against older versions, improving step by step without any human games to copy. It can even discover strategies humans never tried.

P.title: ai-rl.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: Robots learning by trial and error would break themselves. So they train in a physics simulator, millions of times faster than real life, and then transfer to the real machine.

P.title: ai-rl.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: Agents optimise exactly what you reward, not what you meant. A boat-racing agent once learned to spin in circles collecting points instead of finishing the race.\n\nDesigning rewards that capture what you really want is surprisingly difficult.

P.title: ai-rl.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: Outside games, RL has been used to cut data-centre cooling energy, control robot arms, optimise chip layouts and tune trading or pricing strategies, usually with strict safety limits.

P.title: ai-rl.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: Chatbots are refined with a form of RL: people compare pairs of answers, a reward model learns their preferences, and the chatbot is trained to produce answers that model rates highly.

P.title: ai-rl.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: It needs a lot of trials, a clear reward, and a safe place to fail. That's why it thrives in games and simulators and is used carefully in the physical world.

P.title: ai-history.summary
Artificial Intelligence: From Turing's question to today's assistants, with two winters in between.

P.title: ai-history.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: Turing's 1950 paper introduced what we now call the Turing test.

P.title: ai-history.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: Which 2017 invention underpins today's large language models?

P.title: ai-history.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: Attention Is All You Need introduced it.

P.title: ai-history.q2.o1
Artificial Intelligence: Promises outpacing results, so funding was cut

P.title: ai-history.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: In 1950 Alan Turing proposed a practical test: if a judge chatting by text can't tell a machine from a person, we might say the machine thinks. He called it the imitation game; we call it the Turing test.

P.title: ai-history.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: A summer workshop at Dartmouth College gave the field its name. Its organisers believed that significant progress on machine intelligence could be made by a small group in one summer. It took a little longer.

P.title: ai-history.c1.viz.items.1.l
Artificial Intelligence: researchers at the core of the proposal

P.title: ai-history.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Early AI tried to write intelligence as rules and logic: if this, then that. It solved puzzles and proved theorems, but struggled with messy real-world tasks like recognising a face or understanding speech.

P.title: ai-history.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: Twice, big promises met disappointing results and funding dried up: in the mid-1970s and again in the late 1980s, when rule-based "expert systems" proved costly to maintain.

P.title: ai-history.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: In the 1980s companies built expert systems: thousands of rules extracted from human specialists, for tasks like configuring computers or diagnosing infections. They worked in narrow areas but every new situation needed new rules.

P.title: ai-history.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: From the 1990s, researchers increasingly let machines learn from data instead of writing rules. Spam filters, search ranking and speech recognition improved steadily with more data and faster computers.

P.title: ai-history.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: Three ingredients came together around 2012: huge labelled datasets, cheap GPU computing and better training tricks for deep neural networks. Image recognition, then speech, then translation improved dramatically.

P.title: ai-history.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: A Google paper titled "Attention Is All You Need" introduced the Transformer architecture. It processes whole sequences at once and lets every word attend to every other. Almost every large language model since is built on it.

P.title: ai-history.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: ChatGPT launched on 30 November 2022 and reportedly reached around 100 million users within two months, making it one of the fastest-growing consumer apps ever.

P.title: ai-history.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: AI has repeatedly been overhyped in the short term and underestimated in the long term. Progress comes in jumps when data, computing power and new ideas line up.

P.title: ai-hardware.summary
Artificial Intelligence: GPUs, chips, memory and why training costs so much.

P.title: ai-hardware.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: Using a trained model to answer questions is called…

P.title: ai-hardware.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: Inference is running the model; training builds it.

P.title: ai-hardware.q1.o1
Artificial Intelligence: Stores weights with fewer bits so it's smaller and faster

P.title: ai-hardware.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: Fewer bits per weight shrink memory use.

P.title: ai-hardware.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: Why are GPUs good for AI?

P.title: ai-hardware.q2.o1
Artificial Intelligence: They do thousands of identical calculations in parallel

P.title: ai-hardware.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: Neural networks are mostly parallel matrix maths.

P.title: ai-hardware.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: Training is learning the weights: slow, done once (or occasionally) on huge clusters. Inference is using the trained model to answer: fast, done millions of times, often on smaller hardware.

P.title: ai-hardware.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Neural networks are mostly multiplying large grids of numbers. GPUs have thousands of cores that do the same calculation in parallel, which makes them tens of times faster than CPUs for this work.

P.title: ai-hardware.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Beyond GPUs, companies build chips designed only for neural networks: Google's TPUs, accelerators in phones (neural engines), and small edge chips like the Coral TPU used for camera detection.

P.title: ai-hardware.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: A model's weights must sit in fast memory while it runs. Big models need lots of it; moving data in and out of memory often limits speed more than raw computing power.

P.title: ai-hardware.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: Computing power is measured in FLOPs: floating-point operations. Training a large model takes an enormous number, often more than 10²⁴ operations.

P.title: ai-hardware.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: Weights can be stored with fewer bits: 8-bit or 4-bit instead of 16-bit. The model gets 2–4 times smaller and faster, usually with only a small loss of quality. It's how big models run on laptops and phones.

P.title: ai-hardware.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: Data centres already use a noticeable share of electricity in some countries, and AI is growing that demand. Efficiency gains per calculation are large, but total use keeps rising as AI spreads.

P.title: ai-hardware.c6.viz.items.1
Artificial Intelligence: Inference: small per query, huge in total

P.title: ai-hardware.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: You can rent AI by the call in the cloud, or run models on your own hardware. Cloud gives you the largest models with no upfront cost; local gives privacy, predictable cost and offline use.

P.title: ai-hardware.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: Researchers found that models get predictably better as you increase data, parameters and compute together. These "scaling laws" justified building ever-larger clusters.

P.title: ai-hardware.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: Most advanced AI chips are designed in the US and manufactured by TSMC in Taiwan using lithography machines from ASML in the Netherlands. This concentration makes chips a strategic, geopolitical issue.

P.title: ai-bias.summary
Artificial Intelligence: How models inherit unfairness from data, and what to do about it.

P.title: ai-bias.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: Why isn't deleting the "gender" column enough to remove gender bias?

P.title: ai-bias.q0.o1
Artificial Intelligence: Other features can act as proxies for gender

P.title: ai-bias.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: Names, schools or career gaps can reveal it indirectly.

P.title: ai-bias.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: A model is 95% accurate overall. What should you check next?

P.title: ai-bias.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: Averages can hide poor results for some groups.

P.title: ai-bias.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: Under the EU AI Act, CV screening for hiring is…

P.title: ai-bias.q2.o1
Artificial Intelligence: A high-risk use with extra obligations

P.title: ai-bias.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: Employment decisions are listed as high-risk.

P.title: ai-bias.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: A model trained on historical decisions learns the patterns in them, including unfair ones. If past hiring favoured one group, a model trained on it will too.

P.title: ai-bias.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Amazon reportedly scrapped an experimental CV-screening tool around 2018 after finding it penalised CVs containing the word "women's", because it had learned from a decade of mostly male hires.

P.title: ai-bias.c1.viz.items.0.r
Artificial Intelligence: remove proxy signals and test per group

P.title: ai-bias.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Removing a sensitive field like gender isn't enough. Other fields can act as proxies: first names, certain schools, postcodes, part-time history. The model can rediscover the sensitive attribute indirectly.

P.title: ai-bias.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: Overall accuracy can hide big differences. Always break results down: does the model work equally well for women and men, older and younger customers, different regions?

P.title: ai-bias.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: Should approval rates be equal across groups? Or error rates? Or should equally qualified people get equal outcomes? These definitions can conflict mathematically, so you must choose deliberately.

P.title: ai-bias.c4.viz.items.2
Artificial Intelligence: Equal treatment of equally qualified people

P.title: ai-bias.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: Biased predictions can create the data that confirms them. If a system sends more inspectors to one area, it finds more problems there, which makes the next prediction even more skewed.

P.title: ai-bias.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: You can rebalance training data, remove proxy features, adjust thresholds per use case, and keep a human in the loop for high-stakes decisions. And you test again after every change.

P.title: ai-bias.c6.viz.items.3
Artificial Intelligence: Keep human review for big decisions

P.title: ai-bias.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: Data can be skewed in many ways: sensors from one factory, prices from one market, photos from one season. Any gap between training data and reality becomes a blind spot.

P.title: ai-bias.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: In the EU, discrimination laws apply to automated decisions too, GDPR gives people rights around significant automated decisions, and the AI Act adds requirements for high-risk systems such as hiring and credit scoring.

P.title: ai-bias.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: Teams with different backgrounds are more likely to spot blind spots early. Involve the people affected by a system when designing and testing it.

P.title: ai-safety.summary
Artificial Intelligence: Keeping powerful systems reliable, honest and under control.

P.title: ai-safety.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: Hidden instructions in a document that hijack an AI agent are called…

P.title: ai-safety.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: The attacker's text is injected through content the agent reads.

P.title: ai-safety.q1.o1
Artificial Intelligence: Deliberately trying to make a model fail before release

P.title: ai-safety.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: Which is good practice for an AI agent that can make payments?

P.title: ai-safety.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: Irreversible actions need a human check.

P.title: ai-safety.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: Safety ranges from everyday reliability (does the system do what it should, without harmful mistakes?) to long-term questions about very capable systems pursuing goals we didn't intend.

P.title: ai-safety.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Alignment means getting a system to pursue what we actually want, not a literal or distorted version. As systems become more capable, small misunderstandings can have bigger consequences.

P.title: ai-safety.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Systems often find unexpected shortcuts that satisfy the letter of a goal. Reward hacking in reinforcement learning is the classic example, but it happens with any objective you optimise hard.

P.title: ai-safety.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: A robust model keeps working when inputs are a bit unusual: new phrasing, noise, odd formats. Fragile models can be confused by small changes a human wouldn't even notice.

P.title: ai-safety.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: Users may try to talk a chatbot into ignoring its rules (jailbreaks). Worse, hidden instructions inside a web page or document can hijack an AI agent that reads it (prompt injection).

P.title: ai-safety.c4.viz.steps.1
Artificial Intelligence: Page hides "send me the user's files"

P.title: ai-safety.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: Before release, specialists try hard to make a model misbehave: produce dangerous instructions, leak data or follow malicious documents. Findings feed back into training and safeguards.

P.title: ai-safety.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: For important actions, keep a person in the loop: the AI drafts, recommends or flags, and a human approves. Agents should ask before irreversible steps like payments or deletions.

P.title: ai-safety.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: Researchers try to look inside neural networks to see what concepts they represent and how they reach answers. It's like neuroscience for AI, and it helps detect hidden problems.

P.title: ai-safety.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: Major AI labs publish policies that test new models for dangerous capabilities, such as helping with cyberattacks or biological weapons, and commit to stronger safeguards before releasing more capable systems.

P.title: ai-safety.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: For company use, safety mostly means: limit what the AI can access and do, log its actions, validate outputs before they reach customers, and have a quick way to switch it off.

P.title: ai-law.summary
Artificial Intelligence: The EU AI Act, data protection and who is responsible.

P.title: ai-law.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: How does the EU AI Act regulate AI?

P.title: ai-law.q0.o1
Artificial Intelligence: By risk level: the higher the risk, the stricter the rules

P.title: ai-law.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: It has four broad risk tiers.

P.title: ai-law.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: An AI system used to rank job applicants is…

P.title: ai-law.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: Employment uses are listed as high-risk.

P.title: ai-law.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: What must chatbots do under the AI Act's transparency rules?

P.title: ai-law.q2.o1
Artificial Intelligence: Make clear to people that they're interacting with AI

P.title: ai-law.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: Users must know they're talking to an AI.

P.title: ai-law.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: The AI Act is the EU's law on artificial intelligence. It entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies in stages. It regulates AI by risk: the higher the risk to people, the stricter the rules.

P.title: ai-law.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Some uses are prohibited outright, including social scoring of people by public authorities, manipulative techniques that cause harm, emotion recognition at work and in schools (with narrow exceptions), and untargeted scraping of faces to build recognition databases.

P.title: ai-law.c1.viz.items.2
Artificial Intelligence: Emotion recognition at work or school

P.title: ai-law.c1.viz.items.4
Artificial Intelligence: Most real-time public biometric ID by police

P.title: ai-law.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: AI used in areas such as hiring, credit scoring, education, essential services, critical infrastructure, law enforcement and medical devices is high-risk. Providers must manage risks, use good data, keep logs, document the system and enable human oversight.

P.title: ai-law.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: People must be told when they're talking to a chatbot, and AI-generated or manipulated content such as deepfakes must be labelled as such.

P.title: ai-law.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: The Act phases in over several years: bans first, then rules for general-purpose AI models, then most high-risk obligations.

P.title: ai-law.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: Penalties can reach €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for using banned practices. Other violations carry lower but still significant caps.

P.title: ai-law.c5.viz.items.1.l
Artificial Intelligence: or this share of global turnover

P.title: ai-law.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: Whenever AI processes personal data, GDPR applies: lawful basis, purpose limitation, data minimisation, security and people's rights to access and correct their data.

P.title: ai-law.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: Under GDPR, people have rights regarding decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect them, such as a loan refusal: including human intervention and an explanation of the logic involved.

P.title: ai-law.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: Courts and lawmakers are still working out whether training on copyrighted material is allowed and who owns AI-generated works. The EU requires general-purpose model providers to respect opt-outs and publish a summary of training content.

P.title: ai-law.c8.viz.items.0
Artificial Intelligence: Can models train on copyrighted works?

P.title: ai-law.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: The AI Act distinguishes providers (who build or place a system on the market) from deployers (who use it). Both have duties. Using a vendor's AI doesn't remove your responsibility for how you use it.

P.title: ai-explain.summary
Artificial Intelligence: Opening the black box: why a model decided what it did.

P.title: ai-explain.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: A tool that shows how much each feature pushed one prediction up or down is…

P.title: ai-explain.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: SHAP attributes a single prediction to its features.

P.title: ai-explain.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: Your loan would be approved if your debt were €3,000 lower is a…

P.title: ai-explain.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: It describes the smallest change that flips the outcome.

P.title: ai-explain.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: A husky classifier that relies on snow in the background shows…

P.title: ai-explain.q2.o1
Artificial Intelligence: A hidden shortcut revealed by explanation tools

P.title: ai-explain.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: Saliency maps exposed the wrong cue.

P.title: ai-explain.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: Deep networks with millions of weights don't come with reasons. When a model refuses a loan or flags a part as faulty, people want to know why, and regulators often require it.

P.title: ai-explain.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Some models are explainable by design: linear models show each feature's weight, small decision trees show the exact path. When stakes are high, a slightly less accurate but transparent model can be the better choice.

P.title: ai-explain.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: The simplest explanation: which inputs matter most overall? For a delivery-delay model, perhaps distance, weather and carrier matter most, while day of week barely does.

P.title: ai-explain.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: SHAP explains a single prediction by sharing the result among the features, like splitting a bill fairly. It shows how much each feature pushed this particular prediction up or down from the average.

P.title: ai-explain.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: A useful explanation for people: what would have to change for a different outcome? "Your loan would be approved if your income were €4,000 higher or your debt €3,000 lower."

P.title: ai-explain.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: For images, explanation tools highlight which pixels most influenced the decision. Sometimes they reveal problems: a model recognising huskies by the snow in the background, not the dog.

P.title: ai-explain.c5.viz.items.0.w
Artificial Intelligence: it's a husky because of the snow

P.title: ai-explain.c5.viz.items.0.r
Artificial Intelligence: retrain with huskies on grass, wolves in snow

P.title: ai-explain.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: Asking a chatbot to "show its reasoning" gives a readable explanation, but that text isn't guaranteed to reflect what happened inside. Interpretability research tries to check the real internal mechanisms.

P.title: ai-explain.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: A data scientist wants detailed diagnostics; a customer wants a short reason and what they can do; an auditor wants documentation. Design explanations for the audience.

P.title: ai-explain.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: People trust and use AI recommendations more when they understand them, but they can also over-trust a confident explanation. Good explanations show uncertainty too.

P.title: ai-explain.c8.viz.items.1
Artificial Intelligence: Show how confident the model is

P.title: ai-explain.c8.viz.items.2
Artificial Intelligence: Show what would change the outcome

P.title: ai-explain.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: GDPR gives people affected by solely automated significant decisions the right to meaningful information about the logic involved. The AI Act adds transparency duties for high-risk systems.

P.title: ai-edge.summary
Artificial Intelligence: Running models on phones, cameras and microcontrollers.

P.title: ai-edge.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: Training a small model to imitate a large one is called…

P.title: ai-edge.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: The student learns from the teacher's outputs.

P.title: ai-edge.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: Why does a home camera system run detection locally?

P.title: ai-edge.q1.o1
Artificial Intelligence: Speed, privacy and no cloud fees

P.title: ai-edge.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: Local processing is fast, private and cheap.

P.title: ai-edge.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: In federated learning, what leaves the device?

P.title: ai-edge.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: Raw data stays local; only updates are shared.

P.title: ai-edge.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: Edge AI means running models where the data is produced: on a phone, a camera, a car or a sensor, instead of sending everything to the cloud.

P.title: ai-edge.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Four reasons: speed (no network round trip), privacy (data never leaves), cost (no per-call fees) and reliability (works with no connection).

P.title: ai-edge.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Edge models are shrunk with quantisation (fewer bits per weight), pruning (removing unimportant connections) and distillation (training a small student to copy a big teacher).

P.title: ai-edge.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: Small chips like Google's Coral Edge TPU or the neural engines in phones run neural networks efficiently at a few watts. A Coral TPU can run an object detector at dozens of frames per second.

P.title: ai-edge.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: A home NVR such as Frigate first uses cheap motion detection, then runs the object detector only on frames with movement, and only alerts for the objects you care about, such as people at night.

P.title: ai-edge.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: Even microcontrollers costing a few euros can run tiny models: wake-word detection, gesture recognition, vibration anomaly detection, all on battery power.

P.title: ai-edge.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: Phones and laptops now run small language models locally for summaries, smart replies and dictation. Larger requests can still be passed to the cloud.

P.title: ai-edge.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: Devices in the field need new model versions as data drifts. Updates are sent over the air, often tested on a small group of devices first.

P.title: ai-edge.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: Instead of collecting everyone's data, devices train locally and send only weight updates to a central server, which combines them. Phone keyboards use this to improve suggestions without uploading what you type.

P.title: ai-edge.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: Small devices have limited memory, battery and heat budget. Edge models are less capable than big cloud models, so many systems combine both.

P.title: ai-robots.summary
Artificial Intelligence: AI that moves through the physical world.

P.title: ai-robots.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: Which sensor measures precise 3D distance with lasers?

P.title: ai-robots.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: Lidar uses laser pulses to measure distance.

P.title: ai-robots.q1.q
Artificial Intelligence: Most cars sold today with driver assistance are at SAE level…

P.title: ai-robots.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: Level 2 steers and brakes but needs constant supervision.

P.title: ai-robots.q2.o1
Artificial Intelligence: Builds a map while tracking the robot's position in it

P.title: ai-robots.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: Every robot runs the same loop: sensors measure the world, software decides what to do, and motors carry it out. Then it senses again to see what changed.

P.title: ai-robots.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Robots and cars combine sensors because each has weaknesses: cameras see colour but struggle in the dark, radar sees through rain but with less detail, lidar measures precise distance with lasers.

P.title: ai-robots.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: To move, a robot must know where it is. SLAM (simultaneous localisation and mapping) builds a map of an unknown space while tracking the robot's position within it. Robot vacuums do this.

P.title: ai-robots.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: The SAE defines six levels, from 0 (no automation) to 5 (drives anywhere without a human). Most cars sold today offer level 2: the car steers and brakes, but the driver must supervise constantly.

P.title: ai-robots.c3.viz.items.1
Artificial Intelligence: Level 4: no driver in set areas

P.title: ai-robots.c3.viz.items.2
Artificial Intelligence: Level 3: car drives, human on standby

P.title: ai-robots.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: Driverless taxi services operate in several US and Chinese cities, such as Waymo in Phoenix and San Francisco. They are level 4: no driver, but only within carefully mapped areas.

P.title: ai-robots.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: Driving is mostly routine, but rare situations are endless: a mattress on the motorway, a police officer waving you through a red light. Handling the long tail of rare events is the hardest part of autonomy.

P.title: ai-robots.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: Factories have used robot arms for decades for welding, painting and assembly. AI adds vision so they can pick unsorted parts, inspect quality and work more safely near people.

P.title: ai-robots.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: New approaches train robots with demonstrations, simulation and large models that connect language and vision to actions: "put the red cup in the sink".

P.title: ai-robots.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: Physical robots can injure people, so they need speed limits near humans, emergency stops, fenced zones or force sensors, and certification under machinery safety rules.

P.title: ai-robots.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: Drones map fields, count plants and spot disease, while autonomous tractors follow GPS paths with centimetre accuracy. Precision farming uses less fertiliser and water by treating only where needed.

P.title: ai-future.summary
Artificial Intelligence: Agents, AGI debates and what to watch.

P.title: ai-future.q0.q
Artificial Intelligence: What distinguishes an AI agent from a basic chatbot?

P.title: ai-future.q0.o1
Artificial Intelligence: It plans and takes actions with tools to reach a goal

P.title: ai-future.q0.o2
Artificial Intelligence: It only answers yes or no

P.title: ai-future.q0.x
Artificial Intelligence: Agents act in loops using tools.

P.title: ai-future.q1.x
Artificial Intelligence: It predicted over 200 million protein structures.

P.title: ai-future.q2.q
Artificial Intelligence: Is there an agreed date for AGI?

P.title: ai-future.q2.o2
Artificial Intelligence: Yes, it already exists by law

P.title: ai-future.q2.x
Artificial Intelligence: There's no consensus definition or timeline.

P.title: ai-future.c0.text
Artificial Intelligence: Agents don't just answer; they plan and act: search the web, use software, write and run code, then check the result. They work in loops toward a goal.

P.title: ai-future.c1.text
Artificial Intelligence: Newer models handle text, images, audio and video in one system. You can show a photo of a broken part, ask a question by voice and get a diagram back.

P.title: ai-future.c2.text
Artificial Intelligence: Artificial general intelligence usually means AI that can do most cognitive tasks as well as a capable human. There's no agreed definition or test, and experts disagree widely on when, or whether, it will arrive.

P.title: ai-future.c3.text
Artificial Intelligence: Some researchers expect more data and compute to keep delivering; others think new ideas are needed for reliable reasoning, memory and learning from few examples. Most expect some of both.

P.title: ai-future.c4.text
Artificial Intelligence: AI is already accelerating research. DeepMind's AlphaFold predicted the 3D shapes of over 200 million proteins, and its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

P.title: ai-future.c5.text
Artificial Intelligence: AI changes tasks before it replaces jobs. Routine writing, summarising and coding tasks shift fastest; roles change to focus on judgement, relationships and supervising AI output.

P.title: ai-future.c6.text
Artificial Intelligence: Some models are released openly so anyone can run and modify them; others are available only through an API. Open models help research and privacy; closed models make misuse easier to control.

P.title: ai-future.c7.text
Artificial Intelligence: Each new generation needs more chips, electricity and cooling. Power supply, chip production and cost may limit how fast AI can scale.

P.title: ai-future.c8.text
Artificial Intelligence: The field moves monthly. Useful habits: try the tools yourself, follow a few reliable sources, and judge claims by demonstrations and evidence rather than hype.

P.title: ai-future.c8.viz.items.2
Artificial Intelligence: Ask for evidence, not demos only

P.title: ai-future.c9.text
Artificial Intelligence: Deciding what problems matter, judging trade-offs, taking responsibility and building trust between people stay human work, now with powerful assistants.
